transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-31
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Wu (Redwood SE); Jared Cole (Acme - Head of ML Infra), Maya Singh (Acme - SRE), Liam O'Connor (Acme - CTO)

Summary: SE-led deep dive on throughput tuning for production inference. Covered continuous batching, scheduler knob tradeoffs, max_num_seqs and token caps, KV cache behavior, quantization implications, and VPC constraints for a dedicated/private deployment. Actionable tuning recommendations and pilot plan agreed.

Topics: continuous batching; scheduler knobs; max_num_seqs; token limits; KV cache; quantization; VPC/on-prem constraints

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Ethan from our infra team is gonna walk through practical tuning changes to get better throughput without blowing p99s.
[00:12] Ethan: hey hi, hello. quick context - we looked at the short perf spreadsheet Samira shared, and i pulled some synthetic runs to illustrate knobs. i might say kv "cash" at some point, that's my microphone.
[00:30] Jared: cool, yes sorry for the delay folks - juggling two deploys. our main ask: double throughput for chat endpoint while keeping p99 under 350ms. current is around 380 so we hit that spike during peak.
[00:42] Ethan: understood. couple quick Qs about traffic: are you mostly single-turn chat or multi-turn? token distribution?
[00:50] Maya: multi-turn, on average 3.2 turns, token lengths skewed: median 60, 95th around 420, and we have a long tail of >1k tokens for some analysis flows.
[01:05] Liam: also important - we run in a VPC, and need to keep everything on-prem proxied through our firewall; we can do dedicated, but networking overhead matters.
[01:18] Ethan: perfect. i'll go through the knobs in order - continuous batching, scheduler parameters, max_num_seqs, per-request token limits, and KV cache settings. i'll flag which ones are higher risk for latency.
[01:30] Ethan: first continuous batching: Redwood's continuous batching tries to aggregate requests over a short window while still honoring latency SLOs. the main knobs are batch_window_ms and min_batch_size. increasing batch_window_ms from 4ms to 10-12ms can increase token throughput by ~20-30% but impacts tail latency. for your p99 target i would recommend trying 8ms then 10ms if p99 stays ok.
[02:05] Jared: is batch_window_ms applied per model variant or globally?
[02:10] Ethan: per route/model. so you can tune chat differently than embeddings. also there's an adaptive backfill knob - if the scheduler sees underutilization it will wait a bit longer to fill batches. that's scheduler.adaptive_backfill_enable = true/false. enabling it helps throughput at low QPS but can introduce jitter.
[02:34] Maya: jitter hurts us - our customers complain about bursts of latency. how to avoid that?
[02:38] Ethan: you can cap the increase by setting scheduler.max_wait_ms and scheduler.percentile_cutoff. in practice, we set max_wait_ms to 12 and percentile_cutoff to 95 for balanced behavior.
[02:52] Ethan: next, scheduler knobs - there are two important ones: max_batch_size and max_concurrent_batches_per_gpu. max_batch_size should align with GPU memory for sequence length distribution. with your 95th token at 420, i'd recommend conservative max_batch_size of 8 for fp16 kernels, or 12 if you quantize to int8 and have 80GB GPU.
[03:17] Liam: we plan to run on A10-like hardware today but might move to H100 later this year. how do these defaults change?
[03:25] Ethan: H100 can support larger effective batch sizes because of higher mem+bandwidth; you can bump max_batch_size by 1.5-2x depending on sequence length and KV cache size. we also automatically pick kernels based on arch, but you can provide a performance profile override.
[03:40] Ethan: now max_num_seqs - this is a limit on how many concurrent sequences we allocate into a continuous batch for efficiency during decoding. raising it increases throughput but also increases latency variance. for chat-like workloads with many short sequences, increasing max_num_seqs from default 128 to 256 gave Acme-like customers about 35% throughput improvement in our in-house runs. for your mixed long-tail, i'd test 192 first.
[04:08] Jared: what about token limits - can we set per-request caps? we have some users that submit multi-thousand token requests and those blow out our p99.
[04:16] Ethan: yes, token caps are critical. we recommend hard caps at the request router level (e.g., request.max_input_tokens and request.max_output_tokens). you can also add soft-failures (warn + suggest truncation). for your infra i'd suggest max_input 1200, max_output 512 as an initial cap and see how many requests get truncated.
[04:40] Maya: truncation will degrade some analytics workflows, though. any alternatives?
[04:44] Ethan: prefix caching + KV cache can help. if users do repeated context or many overlapping prompts, we can cache prefix KV states; that reduces per-request work. the tradeoff is memory and cache warmup. with long-tail >1k tokens you'll want a larger KV cache pool and longer TTL for the cache entries.
[05:03] Ethan: note - we observed some customers misconfigure kv cache eviction, leading to frequent cache thrash which actually increases latency. set kv.cache_eviction_policy to lru and monitor miss rate; target <10% miss during peak.
[05:17] Jared: how do quantization choices affect throughput vs quality? we've seen 4-bit int8-like quantizashun claims but worried about hallucinations or score drift.
[05:25] Ethan: quantization reduces memory and increases batch capacity. 8-bit quant gives safe throughput gains with minimal quality drop for many LLMs. 4-bit/nn-quant options are more aggressive and need evals. for generation tasks, we typically recommend starting with 8-bit or GPTQ-quant and run a small eval set. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profile per workload.
[05:46] Ethan: another practical tuning is splitting workloads: route latency-sensitive flows to lower-batch, higher-cost pool and throughput-y flows to a high-batch, lower-cost pool. routing is policy-driven (route by label, user tier).
[06:00] Maya: that would help, but adds complexity - do you support automated fallback if dedicated pool fills?
[06:06] Ethan: yes, smart routing and fallback to hosted or different model variants is supported. we also do automatic model variant downgrades when capacity constrained.
[06:16] Jared: can you show config examples?
[06:19] Ethan: sure - (screen share) this is a sample route config: batch_window_ms: 8, scheduler: {max_batch_size: 8, max_concurrent_batches_per_gpu: 2, adaptive_backfill_enable: true, max_wait_ms: 12}, execution: {max_num_seqs: 192, quant_profile: "int8_recommended"}, request_limits: {max_input_tokens: 1200, max_output_tokens: 512}. note: transcript may show braces but our UI surface is YAML like.
[06:58] Jared: i saw you said adaptive backfill - are there metrics to watch?
[07:02] Ethan: yes: batch_fill_ratio, avg_batch_wait_ms, p50/p95 queue_time, and gpu_util. if avg_batch_wait_ms > 15ms increase max_batch_size or drop batch_window_ms. also watch token-per-batch and kv_cache_miss_rate.
[07:18] Liam: on VPC/on-prem - we have extra network hop through our proxy that adds 40-60ms; how much does that eat into p99?
[07:26] Ethan: it matters. network hop is additive to your overall p99. for a 350ms target, a 60ms proxy cost is significant. options: run a dedicated pool within your VPC using Redwood Private (private control plane) to avoid egress hops, or run an on-prem agent. both add operational steps but reduce network latency.
[07:45] Maya: what's the difference in observability if we go private? we need logs, traces for audit.
[07:50] Samira: Private gives customer-managed networking and integrates with your KMS/HSM, audit logs, SSO. Observability is the same Console UX; traces and per-token cost breakdowns still show up but data residency remains in your network. 
[08:05] Jared: perf bench - what should we run?
[08:08] Ethan: three workloads: 1) short-chat (median 60 tokens), 2) mixed (median 120, 95th 420), 3) long-tail analysis (>1k tokens). Run each with baseline config and then with: batch_window_ms=8, max_num_seqs=192, max_batch_size=8, quant=int8. Compare throughput, p50/p95/p99, and kv_cache_miss_rate.
[08:26] Maya: we'll need a script - can you share your harness?
[08:29] Ethan: yes, i'll attach our benchmark harness link and an example k6/postman script for load gen.
[08:34] Jared: any caveats about warmup?
[08:36] Ethan: yes, warmup matters for KV cache and kernel JIT. run a 10-minute warmup at 30% qps before measuring. and for quantized kernels there might be a small cold-start penalty.
[08:49] Ethan: quick tangent - regarding token limits, you can set per-tenant overrides; e.g., power users could get 2k input tokens while free tier gets 512. that's common pattern.
[09:00] Liam: do you have recommendations on auto-scaling? we get sudden spikes from scheduled runs.
[09:05] Ethan: scale on queue length and avg_batch_fill. for dedicated pools, configure a cold standby and warm-up policy so instances don't spin up cold. also use burst capacity for short spikes.
[09:15] Jared: how do we measure effective throughput improvement after changes?
[09:18] Ethan: measure tokens/sec and cost per token, plus p99 latency. our Console has token-level breakdown, you can correlate batch_fill_ratio to cost.
[09:27] Maya: you mentioned kv cache TTL - what's a good starting TTL?
[09:30] Ethan: 5-15 minutes is typical for chat sessions; for long analysis runs you may want 30-60 minutes. tune by watching miss rate and memory pressure.
[09:40] Ethan: let's go through a short example - assume QPS 120, average 3 turns, median 60 tokens. with default knobs you see gpu_util at 55% and token/sec 40k. bumping max_num_seqs to 192 and batch_window to 8ms got to 55k token/sec and gpu_util ~78% in our tests, p99 moved from 320 to 345ms - borderline but still under your target if network hop is low. because you have a 60ms proxy you may cross the line; hence the private pool recommendation.
[10:10] Jared: interesting. what's the rollback story if p99 worsens during A/B?
[10:15] Ethan: we have automatic rollback policies based on latency regression alerts tied to eval prompts. you can set a canary period and a hard p99 budget that triggers instant rollback.
[10:25] Maya: are there any memory leaks or known issues with kv cache staying hot longer than intended?
[10:30] Ethan: historically a few customers mis-set ttl and cache growth happened; we've added eviction safeguards and memory quotas per-model. ensure kv_cache_memory_limit is set per pool.
[10:40] Liam: what about model compilation/jit variability between runs - does that skew perf numbers?
[10:44] Ethan: yes - kernel selection and autotune can cause run-to-run variance. to reduce noise, pin the kernel profile during benchmarking. call it performance_profile: stable_v1.
[10:55] Ethan: question from my side - do you have any legal/reg constraints on data residence that would block Private?
[10:59] Liam: no strict legal blocks, but security team wants KMS integration and audit logs - which you said are supported.
[11:06] Samira: correct, KMS integration and SOC2/ISO artifacts exist; i'll send the security pack.
[11:12] Jared: ok, to recap - we'll run the three benchmark workloads with the proposed config, include a warmup, capture p99/p95/p50, batch_fill_ratio and kv_cache_miss_rate, and share results. we'll also evaluate a dedicated private pool option due to our proxy latency.
[11:26] Ethan: and i'll share the tuning guide and config snippets plus the benchmark harness link.
[11:30] Maya: any last cautions?
[11:32] Ethan: monitor KV cache miss and avg_batch_wait_ms. avoid increasing batch_window_ms beyond 12ms for latency-sensitive routes. and always run a small eval set for quant profiles.
[11:45] Jared: perfect. thanks everybody.
[11:48] Samira: thanks all, i'll follow up with pricing and security docs + next steps.

Notes/imperfections: occasional mis-transcriptions: "kv cash" instead of "KV cache", "quantizashun" for quantization, speaker overlap labeled generically at times. There were a few cross talk bits during config screen share and one spot where the recording shows truncated sentence (approx 32:10 in local recording) but key points above captured.
